items.title: Central registry covers built-in, custom, and MCP tools
items.statement: The canonical tool-support surface includes built-in tools, config-defined custom tools, and MCP-discovered tools; MCP tools are first-class registry entries governed by the same permission and naming rules.

evidence.exact_quote: - **Built-in tools** -- A standard set of tools (bash, edit, read, grep, webfetch, websearch, etc.) with clear semantics, limits, and a unified permission model.

- **MCP** -- MCP tools are **in scope**: they are first-class tools in the central registry; same permission model (including wildcards); naming and precedence with built-in/custom. MCP server config and per-platform config paths are specified in **newtools.md**; live MCP naming, availability, credential, and invalidation vocabulary is specified in **MCP_Integration.md**; here we define how MCP-discovered tools integrate with the registry and policy.

items.title: Settings and Usage expose tool policy and telemetry
items.statement: The GUI requires MCP configuration, per-tool or wildcard allow/deny/ask controls, MVP permission presets, registry-backed tool rows, and a Usage widget for invocation, latency, and error telemetry.

evidence.exact_quote: - **Settings > Permissions** -- **Required:** Per-tool (and optional wildcard) allow/deny/ask; **presets are in scope for MVP** (Read-only, Plan mode, Full) per §10.4 -- user may choose not to apply a preset, but the preset feature must be implemented; list of built-in + MCP-discovered tools with permission dropdown per row. Bound to the same config that the run uses for the central tool registry. Spec: `Plans/Permissions_System.md` §10 and `Plans/FinalGUISpec.md` §7.4 Settings and inspectors.

**Usage page:** Tool usage widget is specified in FinalGUISpec §7.8 (Usage view): tool name, invocation count, latency p50/p95, error rate; data from seglog rollups via analytics scan. See §9.2 enhancement list for context.

items.title: Permission outcomes and precedence are deterministic
items.statement: Tools resolve to allow, deny, or ask; FileSafe remains active after allow, headless ask denies without HITL, precedence is mode through defaults, and last-match-wins applies inside a ruleset.

evidence.exact_quote: - **allow** — Tool may run without prompting. FileSafe guards still apply after permission.
- **ask** — User must approve (`deny` / `once` / `for session` / `for-session` / `always`). In headless runs, maps to `deny` unless HITL is enabled.

Permission rules are evaluated in a deterministic precedence order: Mode override > Session cache > Persona overrides > Project-level > Global-level > Defaults. Within a single ruleset, last-match-wins. Full precedence table: `Plans/Permissions_System.md` §2.4.

items.title: Subagents are canonical child runs with disposable lifecycle
items.statement: A PM subagent is represented as a canonical child run with stable parent/thread identity and requested/effective runtime metadata; provider-native mapping does not alter that identity, and terminal child states normally end the child.

evidence.exact_quote: A PM subagent is a child run. It is not a special-case provider-local actor and it is not defined by provider-native agent-file syntax.
That adapter-level difference does not change the PM child-run canon.
Subagents are disposable by default. Completion, cancellation, or failure normally ends that child. Follow-up work should usually spawn a new child rather than reopen an old one.

items.title: Permission and FileSafe are ordered independent gates
items.statement: Permission is evaluated before FileSafe, so permission to invoke a tool does not authorize a specific invocation; embedded document review cannot bypass those layers through a hidden patch channel.

evidence.exact_quote: FileSafe runs **in addition to** tool permissions. A tool may be **allowed** by permission but still **blocked** by FileSafe. Tool permission = "may the agent call this tool?"; FileSafe = "may this specific invocation proceed?". See `Plans/FileSafe.md`. The policy engine applies both layers in order: permission first, then FileSafe. Full integration order: §10.6.

Embedded document review is not a hidden tool mutation channel. The `embedded-document-pane` consumes the annotation and targeted revision contracts in `Plans/Crosswalk.md`, `Plans/FinalGUISpec.md`, and `Plans/assistant-chat-design.md`; Tools must not introduce direct `patch-apply` or `/suggested-change` mode for that pane unless a later separate capability defines a new tool, permission, FileSafe, and audit contract.

items.title: One policy engine owns every tool attempt
items.statement: Every agent-usable tool attempt resolves identity, permission and approval, invocation validation, terminal binding where relevant, execution, and normalized persistence/analytics output through one ordered engine.

evidence.exact_quote: Every agent-usable tool attempt MUST pass through one canonical policy engine that resolves permission, approval/HITL, FileSafe, execution, terminal binding when relevant, and result normalization.
7. normalize the terminal outcome for persistence, analytics, and reveal-linkback behavior

items.title: Shell execution binds real terminal state
items.statement: Shell-backed execution binds canonical terminal-session state even when hidden, rejected calls do not create fake live sessions, and preview surfaces consume rather than own terminal state.

evidence.exact_quote: - non-interactive or hidden shell execution may suppress opening the terminal UI, but it still binds to canonical terminal-session state when execution actually occurs
- denied or blocked shell calls do not mint fake live terminal sessions

items.title: Tools owns the normalized outcome taxonomy
items.statement: Normalized tool results must distinguish success, runtime error, policy/user/headless/FileSafe/validation rejection, cancellation, timeout, and post-scan failure; Tools owns the taxonomy while storage persists it.

evidence.exact_quote: At minimum, the normalized tool-result taxonomy MUST distinguish:
This document owns the normalized tool-result taxonomy and policy order. Provider docs emit observations; storage docs persist normalized results.

items.title: Routing persists only durable navigation state
items.statement: Historical-result navigation may persist focused-run state, but hover, temporary comparison, and transient pivot interactions must not rewrite persistent view state.

evidence.exact_quote: Tool route activations are persistence-aware. A navigation to a historical-run result may update stored project-state such as `focused_run_id`, while hover previews, temporary comparisons, and transient pivots must not rewrite persistent view state.

items.title: Gap, blocked-state, identity, trust, and graph lineage propagate
items.statement: Tool and route consumers must preserve unresolved gap lineage, blocked recovery fields and freshness, operational identity and export trust state, multi-repository context, governance interception state, scope identity, and node-native runtime evidence; tier fields are compatibility-only projections.

evidence.exact_quote: Tool and route audit records carry unresolved `exact_items` as explicit gap lineage until the owner docs close them. `gap-001` remains tied to the missing owner anchor `### 5.1B Persona/Runtime Snapshot Payload Contract`; `execution_unit_context` consumers must preserve `requested_account_binding`, `requested_account_policy`, and `operational_identity`. `gap-002` keeps `Plans/UI_Command_Catalog.md` references to the non-existent `Plans/Orchestrator_Page.md#10. Search, routing, and action policy` visible until the target exists, and `cmd.search.open_result`, `cmd.search.replace_selected`, and `result_id` remain live search command arguments rather than stale residue. `gap-006` keeps Glossary carry-through honest: help-entry rows use `common_related_states` and must not collapse back into a two-column table.

Blocked-packet consumers in Tools preserve `gap-005`, `/receipt/blocked/usage`, `blocked-attempt`, `blocked_notice`, `blocked-episode`, `/notification`, `report_ref`, `startup_recovered`, `escalation_level`, and `action_available` when a tool or route result exposes blocked runtime state. Runtime recovery surfaces use current projections and valid `allowed_action_ids` / `allowed_action_ids[]`; History and Ledger remain closer to canonical records than widget rollups, while UI consumers expose `Last updated`, `/freshness`, and `/recovery` before actions depend on stale projections. Existing broken anchors such as `Plans/Orchestrator_Page.md#11. Source Control boundary`, `route-target`, `restore points`, `already-recorded` carry-through, and incomplete consumer `carry-through` are tracked as blockers until their owner docs resolve them.

Tool/runtime recovery evidence is `node-native`: blocked episodes, `/evidence/runtime`, and tool-facing usage/evidence/runtime rollups align to graph `/node/package/seam/lane` identity. Any `tier-native` or `tier-aligned` fields survive only as compatibility/grouping projections, never as execution authority.

items.title: Built-in target set spans local, web, and HITL operations
items.statement: The registry target set includes shell, edit-group, file read/search/list, web fetch/search/extract/research/crawl/map, and structured user-question capabilities with canonical permission keys or edit-group sharing.

evidence.exact_quote: The following built-in tools are the **target set** for the central tool registry. Semantics align with [OpenCode's built-in tools](https://opencode.ai/docs/tools/#built-in). Mapping to each platform's native tools (Read/Edit/Bash, etc.) is a Provider/runner concern; the registry holds canonical names and the policy layer applies regardless of provider.

| **question** | Ask the user structured questions during execution | `question` | Supports both single-question and multi-question questionnaire flows. Only meaningful when HITL/UI can show prompts. |

items.title: Edit operations share one permission and ignore semantics
items.statement: Edit, write, patch, and multiedit use a single edit permission, while grep, glob, and list respect .gitignore with project .ignore able to explicitly re-allow paths.

evidence.exact_quote: - **Edit group:** `edit`, `write`, `patch`, and `multiedit` share one **edit** permission so that "allow file changes" is a single knob ([OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/tools/): "The edit permission covers all file modifications (edit, write, patch, multiedit)").

- **Ignore patterns:** grep, glob, list respect `.gitignore` by default. A project **`.ignore`** file can explicitly allow paths (e.g. `!node_modules/`) for search/list. See [OpenCode -- Ignore patterns](https://opencode.ai/docs/tools/#ignore-patterns).

items.title: Debug-capable is cross-surface registry metadata
items.statement: Debug capability is metadata and tagged grouping rather than a new tool ID; eligible built-in, adapter, MCP, skill, and custom tools may join it, all run surfaces may consume it, and classification grants no permission bypass.

evidence.exact_quote: - `debug_capable` is metadata on a tool or capability, not a new tool ID
- Assistant, Interview, Orchestrator, Crew/subagents, and delegated runs may use the same debug-capable tools under the same permission, artifact, and visibility contracts
- classifying a tool as debug-capable does not authorize hidden evidence ingress or bypass the normal permission model

items.title: Stale debug identity requires explicit attention
items.statement: A recoverably stale runtime identity cannot resume silently; tool execution moves to attention_required with the session_reconnect_required reason code.

evidence.exact_quote: - when a debug-capable tool's linked runtime identity is stale but recoverable, tool execution must enter `attention_required` with `attention_required_reason_code = session_reconnect_required` instead of silently resuming against stale sessions

items.title: Provider mappings preserve canonical tool names
items.statement: Provider-native tool names are adapter concerns; policy configuration and registry identity remain canonical so provider additions do not change permission config.

evidence.exact_quote: Providers map canonical tool names to platform-native equivalents (e.g. `edit` → Claude "Edit", Cursor edit tool, etc.). The registry and permission engine use **canonical names only**; platform_specs or runner code holds the mapping so that adding a new provider does not require changing permission config.

items.title: LSP exposes nine reads and one approval-gated rename
items.statement: Canonical LSP offers nine named read/navigation operations and rename as the single write operation; short lookup names and lsp_rename are compatibility aliases, workspaceSymbol requires query, position operations use path and position, and status is normalized.

evidence.exact_quote: Canonical operation inventory: the packetization summary phrase `10 read-only + 1 write-gated (lsp_rename)` reconciles to the live Part M operation set as nine read-only operations plus one approval-gated `rename` operation. `lsp_rename` is a legacy/source alias for canonical `rename` / `lsp.rename`, not a second tool key.

Short LSP lookup names `definition`, `references`, and `implementation` are compatibility aliases for `goToDefinition`, `findReferences`, and `goToImplementation`; the canonical operation names remain the long-form LSP actions above.
- ok | partial | unavailable | error

items.title: Tool adapters normalize sync behavior, recovery, previews, and settlement
items.statement: Tool adapters default to synchronous execution unless async handles are explicit; blocked calls include structured recovery, previews use source/result or diff mini-cards without becoming mutations, and settlement_state follows an ordered nine-value precedence.

evidence.exact_quote: All core tool-contract (`/tool-contract`) adapters default to sync execution semantics unless/until a tool contract explicitly exposes async handles. When a call is blocked by permissions, FileSafe, or an unavailable MCP/service (`/service`), the result must include a structured recovery action rather than a passive error only. Non-terminal operation previews use the same mini-card family as terminal output: web/search results show source/result mini-cards, and code-edit previews expose `/diffs` cards that open the editor diff without treating the preview as the final mutation. Built-in tool contracts must keep concrete `I/O/limit/error` guidance, unknown-tool default handling, GUI permission/preset visibility (`/presets`), and usage `/token` / `/tokens` event linkage discoverable from this registry.

`ToolTurnSettlement` uses the wire field `settlement_state`. Allowed values are `success`, `partial`, `partial_truncated`, `malformed`, `nullable_content`, `redacted`, `retained`, `retryable`, and `fatal`. Precedence when multiple conditions apply is: `fatal` > `malformed` > `partial_truncated` > `redacted` > `nullable_content` > `partial` > `retryable` > `retained` > `success`. `success` is legal only when required result, error, truncation, retention, and redaction metadata have been normalized and persisted or intentionally omitted by the specific tool contract.

items.title: Bash supports sync, async, reuse, and bounded initial wait
items.statement: Bash requires command text, defaults to sync, supports async and shell reuse, validates initial_wait in the closed integer range 1 through 300, returns completed or running envelopes, and distinguishes validation, policy, FileSafe, shell, spawn, output, and timeout errors.

evidence.exact_quote: | `mode` | enum (`"sync"` \| `"async"`) | no | Execution mode. Default `sync`. `sync` waits through `initial_wait`; `async` returns immediately with a live shell handle. |

| `initial_wait` | integer seconds | no | Sync-mode wait window before returning partial output and a running shell handle. Default `30`; minimum `1`; maximum `300`; values outside this closed range are `validation_error`. |
- Completed sync result: `{ shellId, status: "completed", stdout, stderr, exit_code }`

items.title: Bash timeout separates wait expiry from hard termination
items.statement: Expiry of initial_wait returns a live running shell with partial output, while hard-ceiling expiry terminates the process and returns a timed_out envelope with null exit code.

evidence.exact_quote: - If `initial_wait` expires first, the command remains live and returns `status: "running"` with partial `stdout` / `stderr`.
- If the hard execution ceiling expires, the runtime terminates the process and returns `{ shellId, status: "timed_out", stdout, stderr, exit_code: null, error: { code: "timeout" } }`.

items.title: Edit performs exact atomic replacement with reveal metadata
items.statement: Edit requires an allowed-root path and exact old/new strings, reports replacement spans and byte/line deltas, distinguishes validation/policy/path/match/encoding/timeout failures, and guarantees no partial rewrite on timeout.

evidence.exact_quote: | `path` | string | yes | Target file path. Must resolve inside an allowed workspace root. |
`{ status: "success", path, replacements: [{ start_line, end_line }], line_count_changed, bytes_changed }`
- On timeout, the operation must fail atomically: no partial file rewrite, and the response is `{ status: "timed_out", path, error: { code: "timeout" } }`.

items.title: Provider view normalizes to canonical read
items.statement: Provider-native view maps to read, accepts a path and optional inclusive one-based range with -1 meaning EOF, returns distinct structured file or directory envelopes, preserves line numbering, and defines validation, policy, path, binary, size, and timeout errors.

evidence.exact_quote: Provider-native `view` maps to the canonical registry tool `read`.
| `view_range` | array `[start_line, end_line]` | no | Inclusive 1-based line range. `-1` as `end_line` means "to end of file". |
- File read: `{ path, kind: "file", content, lines: [{ line_number, text }], truncated? }`
- Directory read: `{ path, kind: "directory", entries: string[] }`

items.title: Normalized outcome and settlement taxonomies lack a mapping
items.statement: The window defines a tool-result taxonomy and a separate settlement_state taxonomy, but gives no deterministic mapping between outcomes such as permission_denied, timed_out, or post_scan_failure and settlement values such as fatal, retryable, partial, or retained.
items.impact: Providers, persistence, analytics, and UI can classify the same terminal tool attempt differently even though both taxonomies claim normalization authority.
items.builder_discretion: Builders must invent outcome-to-settlement mapping rules and decide whether one or both fields drive terminal interpretation.

evidence.exact_quote: At minimum, the normalized tool-result taxonomy MUST distinguish:

`ToolTurnSettlement` uses the wire field `settlement_state`. Allowed values are `success`, `partial`, `partial_truncated`, `malformed`, `nullable_content`, `redacted`, `retained`, `retryable`, and `fatal`. Precedence when multiple conditions apply is: `fatal` > `malformed` > `partial_truncated` > `redacted` > `nullable_content` > `partial` > `retryable` > `retained` > `success`. `success` is legal only when required result, error, truncation, retention, and redaction metadata have been normalized and persisted or intentionally omitted by the specific tool contract.

items.statement: The LSP rules require preservation of a normalized result envelope, but the authoritative core enumerates only generic fields and status labels; it does not define result payload fields or per-operation response shapes.
items.impact: Adapters can emit incompatible definition, reference, symbol, hover, call-hierarchy, and rename results, preventing reliable persistence and agent-visible normalization.
items.builder_discretion: Builders must invent the LSP result envelope and operation-specific payload schemas.

items.statement: The core names query, path, position, newName, and status and states broad applicability rules, but does not define their types, the position structure, or the complete required/optional field matrix for each operation.
items.impact: Provider adapters can disagree on URI versus path, line/column bases, position encoding, and validation for document symbols and call-hierarchy operations.
items.builder_discretion: Builders must select field types, coordinate bases, encodings, and per-operation validation rules.

items.title: Bash output overflow policy is non-deterministic
items.statement: The output_limit_exceeded error permits either truncation or process abort but gives no cap, selection rule, required truncation metadata, or relationship to a still-running shell.
items.impact: Identical commands can have different liveness and data-loss behavior across runners, and consumers cannot reliably distinguish retained partial output from aborted execution.
items.builder_discretion: Builders choose output caps, whether overflow truncates or aborts, and what recovery metadata is emitted.

evidence.exact_quote: | `output_limit_exceeded` | Output exceeded cap and was truncated or the command was aborted per runtime policy. |

items.title: Bash hard execution ceiling is advisory and underspecified
items.statement: The only hard-ceiling value is recommended rather than required and permits an unspecified stricter runner limit without naming its config key, minimum, visibility, or persistence in the result.
items.impact: Users and agents cannot predict when a shell process will be forcibly terminated, and different runners can silently apply different ceilings.
items.builder_discretion: Builders choose whether 30 minutes is enforced, where overrides live, and how the effective limit is surfaced.

evidence.exact_quote: - Recommended hard execution ceiling: `30m` per shell command unless a stricter runner limit is configured.

items.title: Detached bash lifecycle lacks ownership and recovery rules
items.statement: Detach declares that a process survives client shutdown but does not specify owner identity, later discovery or reattachment, cancellation authority, retention, or cleanup after the originating client disappears.
items.impact: Detached processes can become orphaned, inaccessible, or ambiguously owned, creating resource, security, and audit risks.
items.builder_discretion: Builders must invent detached-process ownership, persistence, reconnection, cancellation, and garbage-collection behavior.

evidence.exact_quote: | `detach` | boolean | no | Async-only. When `true`, the process is fully detached and survives client shutdown; when `false`, it remains attached to the shell session. |

items.title: Read range behavior for directory targets is undefined
items.statement: The same path parameter may identify a file or directory, but the optional line-based view_range has no validity or ignore rule for directory reads.
items.impact: Adapters can reject, ignore, or misapply view_range on directories, yielding incompatible validation and UI behavior.
items.builder_discretion: Builders choose whether a directory plus view_range is validation_error or whether the range is ignored.

evidence.exact_quote: | `path` | string | yes | File or directory path to inspect. |
| `view_range` | array `[start_line, end_line]` | no | Inclusive 1-based line range. `-1` as `end_line` means "to end of file". |

items.title: Edit miss and conflict codes overlap
items.statement: replace_miss is described as old_str not being found exactly once, which includes multiple matches, while replace_conflict separately owns multiple ambiguous matches; the discriminator is not exact.
items.impact: Equivalent multi-match failures can normalize to different codes, weakening deterministic recovery and analytics.
items.builder_discretion: Builders choose whether multiple matches produce replace_miss or replace_conflict and what counts as ambiguity.

evidence.exact_quote: | `replace_miss` | `old_str` was not found exactly once as required by the tool contract. |
| `replace_conflict` | Multiple ambiguous matches or file changed during validation. |

items.title: Tool Usage metrics lack aggregation semantics
items.statement: The widget names invocation count, latency percentiles, and error rate but does not define time window, project/run scope, inclusion rules, percentile population, or what outcomes count as errors.
items.impact: Usage views can display materially different metrics from the same seglog data and cannot be validated against one oracle.
items.builder_discretion: Builders choose aggregation window, scope, denominators, and error classification.

evidence.exact_quote: **Usage page:** Tool usage widget is specified in FinalGUISpec §7.8 (Usage view): tool name, invocation count, latency p50/p95, error rate; data from seglog rollups via analytics scan. See §9.2 enhancement list for context.

dimension_assessments.summary: Canonical registry, routing, policy, terminal, debug, and core tool behaviors are explicit.
Built-in, custom, MCP, debug-capable, LSP, web, structured-question, and edit-group capability families are identified.
Bash, edit, and read have concrete envelopes, but LSP parameter/result schemas and some parameter combinations remain incomplete.
Central policy and per-tool contracts are substantial, but taxonomy mapping, LSP schemas, limit policy, and overlapping edit errors are under-specified.
Child-run disposal, policy resolution, shell running/completed/timed_out, and stale-debug attention transitions are explicit; detached-process lifecycle is not.
Tools owns policy order and normalized outcomes, providers own native mapping observations, storage owns persistence, and tier projections cannot become execution authority.
Registry, provider mapping, storage, and terminal ownership are stated, but detached-process ownership after client shutdown is absent.
Assistant, Interview, Orchestrator, Crew/subagents, delegated runs, chat cards, Usage, History, Ledger, recovery widgets, and storage/analytics consumers are named with carry-through duties.
Required permission and MCP settings plus tool telemetry are stated, but Usage metric aggregation semantics are not testable from this core.

Policy, FileSafe, shell, edit, read, LSP unavailable, attention-required, timeout, and structured recovery paths are covered, but output overflow, detached recovery, and error-code overlap remain ambiguous.
Permission, FileSafe, sensitive-path guards, allowed workspace roots, web URL controls, approval gating, and the no-hidden-ingress rule establish security boundaries.
Gap lineage, blocked state, freshness, identity, trust, multi-context, governance, scope, and node-native evidence are explicitly preserved through tool consumers.
Operational order, terminal binding, provider normalization, sync/async shell execution, and atomic edit behavior are defined; detached lifecycle and hard timeout authority are not complete.
Initial wait bounds, recommended execution ceiling, search index fallback, size/depth/fan-out concepts, and Usage percentiles exist, but output caps and analytics windows lack deterministic values.
Provider-native tool mappings, view/read, LSP short names and lsp_rename, OpenCode baseline context, and tier compatibility projections have explicit canonicalization rules.

Exact status values, envelopes, validation ranges, atomicity, and error codes provide many oracles, but LSP output, taxonomy mapping, overflow behavior, and Usage aggregation lack single expected results.
Material discretion remains in taxonomy mapping, LSP schemas, output overflow, hard timeouts, detached lifecycle, directory-range handling, edit error classification, and telemetry aggregation.
Nine bounded ambiguities are evidenced within the authoritative core; none depends on context-after lines or unrelated sources.
